mstts:express-as.prosody: Welcome to this journey—one that asks us to quietly question all the expectations shaping our daily lives. Imagine, just for a moment, what it might feel like to let go of the pressure to fit in, and instead, listen to that wild, authentic voice inside you—the one that's often drowned out by the world telling you how you should be. In Glennon Doyle’s Untamed, we get to explore what happens when we move from self-denial to self-discovery—redrawing the boundaries of who we are, who we love, and the truths we choose to live by. Together, we’ll look at what it really means to trust our own intuition, to honor our desires even when it feels risky, and to see vulnerability not as weakness, but as an act of real courage. As we peel back the layers of conditioning, a new kind of freedom comes into focus—one where honesty, compassion, and fierce self-respect can guide every step we take. Through stories of heartbreak, transformation, and deep acceptance, Untamed invites us to imagine a life that feels true and unrestrained—not just for ourselves, but for everyone we inspire along the way. So, if you’re ready to question the cages you live in and open up to a more vibrant, connected existence, you’re in exactly the right place. Let’s set out together, and discover what it really means to become untamed.

Chapter 1: Learning to Question the Rules That Shape a Life.
Have you ever noticed how most of us grow up surrounded by invisible instructions? These aren’t written down anywhere, but they guide us all the same—woven into our families’ routines, the lessons at school, even the quiet expectations from friends and neighbors. As kids, we pick up on what it means to be “good.” Usually, that means being quiet, helpful, and agreeable. And before you know it, these little lessons settle in, shaping how we walk through the world.
For one woman, the urge to fit in was there right from the start. She learned to read the room, to sense what everyone wanted from her, and to deliver it—almost like second nature. At home, she tried hard to be the daughter her parents could brag about. At school, she worked to be liked, to avoid trouble. Even as a teenager, when things got confusing and overwhelming, she held on to the idea that following the rules would keep her safe.
But here’s the thing: the rules kept changing. Suddenly, the pressure to be thin, pretty, and popular grew louder and louder. She started to notice how girls were praised for shrinking themselves—physically, yes, but emotionally too. The message was everywhere: don’t take up too much space. Don’t be too loud, too opinionated, or too needy. She watched friends learn to hide their real feelings, to laugh when the joke wasn’t funny, to pretend everything was fine—even when it wasn’t.
Adulthood only piled on more expectations. Now, being “good” meant being a devoted partner, a selfless mom, a reliable friend, and a productive worker. The list of shoulds just kept growing. And the cost of breaking any rule? It felt higher than ever. She tried to keep up. Still, deep down, there was this quiet ache—like she was living someone else’s life.
Then, one ordinary day at the zoo with her daughter, something changed. She watched a cheetah pacing inside its cage. The animal was stunning—so powerful—but it just moved in tight circles, following the same path over and over. The cheetah’s wildness was still there, but it had been tamed, trained to perform, to obey, to fit into a world that wasn’t made for it. And suddenly, she saw herself in that cheetah. She realized how she, too, had learned to ignore her instincts and desires.
Most of us don’t realize how much of our lives are shaped by these invisible cages. The rules are so familiar, they just feel like the truth. But sometimes, out of nowhere, there’s a moment of clarity—a spark that says, life could be different. The longing for freedom, for something real, starts as a whisper. It asks, What if the rules aren’t right? What if the life that feels safe is actually just too small?
This realization doesn’t usually hit all at once. It’s a slow build, made up of little acts of noticing. Maybe a mom catches herself telling her child to be quiet when, deep down, she really wants to hear what they have to say. Or a friend feels a pang of envy when someone else dares to speak their mind. Maybe a partner wonders why they always say yes—when their heart is screaming no. These moments, as uncomfortable as they are, are actually invitations. They’re a chance to question, to imagine, to start again.
The journey toward untaming? It always starts with curiosity. It’s about looking at the rules you’ve inherited and asking, Who really benefits from these? It encourages a gentle rebellion—a willingness to listen to that quiet voice inside that says, There’s more to life than this. For many, that’s the very first step toward a life that finally feels true, free, and entirely their own.

Chapter 2: Listening to the Voice Within and Trusting Its Wisdom
After years of following everyone else’s rules, it’s easy to lose touch with what’s real for you. The world is noisy, isn’t it? There’s advice coming from every direction—how to live, how to love, how to succeed. It’s almost second nature to look outside ourselves for answers, trusting experts, traditions, or just hoping for approval.
But underneath all that noise, there’s another kind of knowing. It’s quiet, steady—and it speaks in feelings, gut instincts, and even dreams.
Let me share a story with you. There was a woman who, for years, had tuned out her own needs. Whenever life handed her big decisions—about marriage, becoming a mother, or her career—she’d ask everyone else what she should do. She wanted to be sure, to find some guarantee that her choices were right. But the more she searched outside herself, the more lost she felt.
Everything started to shift when she began noticing her own discomfort. She realized her body would tense up whenever she said yes to things she didn’t want. She felt a heaviness in her chest whenever she pretended to be happy. And suddenly, it clicked—her anxiety wasn’t a sign that something was wrong with her. It was a signal. Her body was telling her she was living out of sync with her own truth.
One evening, alone in a quiet room, she tried something different. Instead of reaching for her phone or asking a friend, she just closed her eyes and listened. At first, all she could hear was static—worries, doubts, and echoes of everyone else’s voices. But as she sat there, letting herself feel uncomfortable, something shifted. A new kind of clarity started to emerge. She remembered what it felt like to want something for herself, with no need to apologize or explain.
Think about it—most of us are taught to distrust our own desires. Maybe you’ve heard that wanting too much is selfish, or that strong feelings can get you into trouble. We’re told it’s safer to be practical than passionate. But here’s something to pay attention to: your inner voice is wise. It truly knows what brings you joy, what feels wrong, and what’s really worth fighting for. It doesn’t always come through as words. Sometimes, it feels like lightness, a spark of energy, or just a quiet sense of peace.
Learning to trust that voice? It takes practice. You have to carve out moments of silence, even when the world is shouting at you. You start to notice the difference between fear and intuition—the urge to just stay safe, and the gentle nudge that’s calling you to grow. And you learn to honor your feelings, even when nobody else gets it.
There will be times when listening to your inner voice leads to tough choices. You might realize a relationship isn’t working, even though it looks perfect from the outside. Or maybe, as a parent, you decide to set boundaries—even if it means someone ends up disappointed. You might even walk away from a stable job to chase a dream that seems risky. These aren’t easy decisions, but they’re honest. They come from a place of self-respect and trust.
Over time, this way of listening becomes a way of life. It isn’t about being impulsive or reckless. It’s about being real. It’s about truly believing that happiness and fulfillment aren’t just for other people—they’re for anyone who’s willing to listen to themselves. The world might not always get it, but that’s okay. The reward? A life that’s grounded, genuine, and completely your own.

Chapter 3: Embracing Imperfection and the Power of Vulnerability
You know, perfection can be a really tempting idea. It whispers that if we just get everything right, we’ll finally be safe, accepted, even loved. Most of us learn early on that making mistakes isn’t okay, that flaws are something to hide, and showing vulnerability? Well, that’s often seen as a weakness.
The pressure to be perfect is everywhere—especially when you’re led to believe that your worth depends on your performance, your looks, or how much you give to others. Sound familiar?
Let me tell you about one woman who tried to cope with pain by chasing perfection. Whenever life felt out of control, she focused on controlling herself—her body, her emotions, even her relationships. She truly believed that if she could just do everything “right,” peace would finally follow. But the more she tried to hold it all together, the more anxious and disconnected she felt.
Then came a crisis. Her marriage was falling apart, her sense of self was shaky, and she felt so alone in her struggles. She was exhausted from pretending, from always trying to fit the image of a “good” wife, mother, or friend. One day, she just couldn’t fake it anymore. She let her guard down and told a close friend the truth—she was struggling, she didn’t have all the answers, and honestly, she was scared.
And you know what? The world didn’t fall apart. Her friend responded with kindness and understanding. That moment—sharing her pain and letting herself be seen in all her imperfection—brought a huge sense of relief. Suddenly, it became crystal clear: vulnerability wasn’t weakness. It was actually a bridge. It opened the door to real connection, empathy, and healing.
Most people are afraid to let their true selves show. There’s this worry that if others see the mess, they’ll turn away or judge us. But here’s the thing—everyone’s dealing with something. Everyone has moments of doubt, fear, or failure. And when one person has the courage to be honest about their struggles, it gives everyone else permission to be real, too.
Embracing imperfection? It doesn’t mean you stop growing. It just means you accept that being human is messy, and real strength comes from facing life as it is—not how we think it “should” be. It’s about letting go of needing to have it all together, and choosing to be authentic instead.
In relationships, vulnerability is what creates true intimacy. When partners, friends, or family members open up about their fears and hopes, they make room for real trust and understanding. And when parents admit their mistakes, they teach their kids something powerful—that it’s okay to be imperfect. Love doesn’t depend on being flawless.
Over time, that woman I told you about learned to see her imperfections as just part of her story. She stopped apologizing for her feelings, her needs, and her dreams. She realized the people who mattered most didn’t just love her in spite of her flaws—they cherished her honesty and courage. And in that freedom to be imperfect, she found a peace that chasing perfection could never offer.

Chapter 4: Redefining Motherhood, Partnership, and Family on Authentic Terms
You know, family is often seen as the ultimate test of selflessness. As parents, we’re told to put our kids first—sacrifice our own needs, keep the peace, and just hold it all together, no matter what. Partners are supposed to be steady, supportive, and always reliable. The roles feel so clear... and the rules? They can be strict.
But what happens when all those expectations start clashing with your own longing to live honestly and fully?
There was one mother who really wrestled with this tension every single day. She loved her children with all her heart, but she also craved a life that felt true to who she was. She wanted to set an example—not just by providing for her family, but by showing her kids what it looks like to be brave, to take chances, and to actually follow your heart.
Things got especially real when her marriage began to unravel. Suddenly, she had to choose: stay in a relationship that looked good from the outside but felt empty inside, or risk it all for a shot at genuine happiness. And that choice wasn’t just about her—it was about her kids, her partner, and the life they’d built together.
Most of us assume the best parents are the ones who sacrifice everything for their children. But over time, something became clear—kids learn so much more from what we do than from what we say. When a parent chooses honesty over comfort, or personal growth over just playing it safe, it teaches children to trust themselves. It shows them it’s possible to love others without completely losing who you are.
Redefining family meant letting go of the idea that there’s only one right way to be a mother, a partner, or even a friend. It called for new traditions, fresh boundaries, and some hard but necessary conversations. Sometimes, love means letting go. And real connection? Well, it’s built on truth—not just obligation.
Through it all, this woman discovered something surprising: her children were more resilient than she ever imagined. They didn’t need her to be perfect—they just needed her to be real. They needed to see her struggle, watch her make mistakes, and witness her getting back up again. They needed to know it’s okay to change, to grow, and to choose a different path, even if it’s scary.
Partnership was reimagined, too. Instead of seeing love as a contract or a duty, it became a choice—something you decide to show up for, every single day. It was about listening, supporting each other’s growth, and allowing space for both closeness and independence. It wasn’t always easy, but it was honest. And that honesty created room for both commitment and freedom.
In the end, family became less about roles, and so much more about relationships. It was about showing up as your true self—and inviting others to do the same. The goal became building a home where everyone was free to be themselves—messy, complicated, and wonderfully real.

Chapter 5: Claiming Identity and Embracing the Fullness of Self
You know, identity isn’t simple. It’s this mix of family, culture, beliefs, and all the little things life throws at us. Most of the time, it feels a whole lot easier just to blend in—to hide those parts of ourselves that don’t quite match what everyone expects. But have you ever noticed what that really costs us? When we hide, we end up feeling lonely, ashamed, almost like we’re living someone else’s life.
Let me share a story. There was a woman who always felt a bit different, but she tried to brush it off. She married young, started a family, built a life that, on paper, looked pretty perfect. But deep down, she was restless. There was this hidden piece of her that was longing for more—something real and honest.
Everything changed one day, almost by accident. She met someone who made her feel truly alive, in ways she’d never known before. The connection was powerful, but it didn’t fit the story she’d always believed about herself—or the one others expected her to live. She was scared. What would it mean to own up to this new truth? She worried about hurting her family, letting down her community, maybe even losing everything she’d built.
But the pull to be authentic—to finally live honestly—was stronger than her fear. She realized, she just couldn’t keep pretending. She wanted to be seen, really seen, for who she was. She wanted to love and be loved, not for the mask she wore, but for the person she truly was inside.
Coming out wasn’t easy. There were tough moments—grief, loss, uncertainty. But there was also joy. It felt like coming home to herself. She discovered that the people who genuinely loved her cared about her happiness, even if it meant letting go of old dreams. She found new friends, new communities, and a whole new sense of belonging.
So often, we underestimate what it means to live honestly. We think that if we just fit in, we’ll find peace—but really, that only leads to emptiness. Real belonging comes from being seen and accepted, just as we are. It means owning every part of ourselves—the strengths, the struggles, the dreams, and even those nagging doubts.
Over time, this woman learned to truly celebrate her identity. She stopped apologizing for her desires, her ambitions, her needs. She realized her story mattered—not only for herself, but for anyone else searching for the courage to be real. She became a beacon of hope, living proof that it’s never too late to start over, to take a new path, and to build a life that actually feels like your own.

Chapter 6: The Courage to Disappoint Others and Stand in Your Truth.
Have you ever felt torn between keeping the peace and just being real? There’s this quiet moment—almost like standing at a trembling crossroads—where you feel pulled between what others want from you, and what you know deep down is true for you. Most of us? We’d rather not face it. The fear of letting people down is powerful. It can keep you stuck in jobs you’ve outgrown, relationships that don’t fit anymore, or routines that just drain you—all because you want to keep everyone happy.
I want to share a story about a woman who knew that fear all too well. For years, she became an expert at smoothing over conflict. She’d say yes, even when her heart screamed no. She got so used to shrinking herself to fit everyone else’s expectations. The idea of disappointing her parents, her partner, or her friends? It felt unbearable. She believed love was all about sacrifice, and her own needs—well, they just had to wait.
But here’s what happened. The cost of ignoring herself just kept growing. She started noticing resentment building up. Exhaustion became her constant companion. Her own dreams, the things that once lit her up, started to fade into the background. The more she tried to be everything for everyone, the less she recognized the person staring back in the mirror.
One afternoon, after a tough conversation with someone she loved, she found herself sitting alone in her car, tears streaming down her face. The ache in her chest? All too familiar. But this time, instead of pushing it away, she let herself feel it. She allowed the full weight of her disappointment—not just in others, but in herself—to settle in. And that’s when it hit her: the only way forward was to risk being misunderstood.
Here’s something to really pay attention to—most people don’t realize that sometimes, disappointing others is necessary. It’s not about being selfish or unkind; it’s about honoring your own truth. When you choose honesty over approval, it can feel like you’re betraying someone. But in reality, it’s an act of self-respect. It’s you saying, “Hey, my life matters, too.”
The first time she said no to something that didn’t feel right, her hands literally shook. She worried about the fallout—worried that people would think she was difficult or ungrateful. But you know what? The world didn’t end. Some people were upset, sure. But others actually respected her boundaries. She learned that real relationships can handle disappointment—that love doesn’t have to mean erasing yourself.
Over time, she started trusting herself more. She realized her worth wasn’t measured by how much she could give, or how little she could need. There was real freedom in simply telling the truth—even when it was hard. That courage to disappoint others? It became the foundation for a life that finally felt honest and whole.
So, here’s the truth: we all face moments when what’s real for us doesn’t match what others expect. And yeah, it’s never easy. But the alternative—living with quiet resentment and regret—is so much harder. The path to freedom starts with one brave step: choosing to honor your own voice, even if it means letting someone down.

Chapter 7: Reclaiming Joy, Pleasure, and the Right to Want More
There’s something quietly rebellious about letting yourself want more, isn’t there?
For so long, so many of us have been told that desire is dangerous. That asking for more is greedy. That pleasure is just a distraction—and joy? Something you’re supposed to earn through hard work and sacrifice.
The world loves to whisper, “Just be grateful for what you already have. Don’t push your luck.”
I want you to picture someone—a woman who grew up with these ideas woven deep into her story. She learned to quiet her own longings, to settle for “good enough,” and to feel guilty just for wanting anything extra. She saw it all around her too—friends stuck in jobs that drained them, parents shelving their dreams, and partners who forgot what being truly alive even felt like.
But here’s the thing about desire: it never really disappears. It sneaks back in through daydreams, catches you off-guard with a twinge of envy, or lingers as that gentle ache for something different.
For years, she tried to hush that voice, thinking contentment meant making peace with less. But no matter how hard she tried, the longing never left.
Then one day, as she watched her children play outside, everything shifted. Their joy was so pure—unfiltered and free. They laughed, chased, and reached for what they wanted, no apologies, no shame. It hit her: joy isn’t something we have to earn. It’s our birthright.
Somewhere along the way, most of us forget how to play, how to savor, how to simply want. We swap pleasure for productivity, convinced that rest and delight are luxuries we can’t afford. But honestly? Joy is essential. It’s what gives life its spark. It’s what fuels our creativity, connects us to others, and helps us bounce back when things get tough.
Reclaiming joy meant daring to want more—not just for herself, but for everyone she cared about. It meant saying yes to the things that made her feel alive, even if they looked a little impractical or indulgent. It meant trusting that her own desires weren’t something to fix or hide—they were clues, pointing her toward what really matters.
Of course, the old guilt didn’t just vanish overnight. Habits like that take time to unlearn. But with each act of self-acceptance, that guilt faded a little more. She started to celebrate her happiness, savor little pleasures, and chase after dreams that once felt impossible.
Most people don’t realize just how powerful joy really is. They think it’s a distraction from “real life,” but honestly, joy is the work. It’s the fuel that makes everything else possible.
Your right to want more? It’s not selfish. It’s a bold declaration of hope—a refusal to settle for anything less than a life that’s vibrant and fully lived.

Chapter 8: Navigating Grief, Loss, and the Art of Letting Go
Loss—it’s something we all face sooner or later, even if we wish we could avoid it. The pain of letting go, whether it's a relationship, a cherished dream, or even a part of who we thought we were, can just feel overwhelming. Isn’t it tempting to hold on, to pretend nothing’s changed, or to keep so busy that you don’t have to feel that ache?
Think of a woman who found herself riding the waves of grief. It started with her marriage ending, then losing old friends, and finally, the heavy realization that some of the dreams she had were never going to come true. At first, she tried to outrun it all—filling her days with distractions, hoping the sadness would just disappear if she stayed busy enough.
But here’s the thing—grief is patient. It waits. It shows up in those quiet moments, when no one else is around. Maybe it’s a song on the radio, a scent in the air, or just a memory that sneaks up when you least expect it. She spent a long time resisting, scared that if she really let herself feel that loss, she might never recover.
Then, one evening, when the house was finally silent, she sat with her sorrow. She let herself cry. Let the memories wash through her. She allowed herself to mourn everything she’d lost. It was messy—raw, even—but it was real. And in that honest moment, she realized something: grief wasn’t her enemy. It was actually proof that she’d loved deeply, that she’d dared to hope.
So often, we’re told to hide our pain. To “move on” as quickly as possible. To be strong for everyone else. But here’s something important—healing only happens when we feel. When we let our hearts break and trust that, with time, they’ll mend. Letting go isn’t just about saying goodbye to what was; it’s about making space for what might be.
And letting go? It’s not a one-and-done deal. It’s something you practice. Every day, you release a little more. You forgive. You surrender, even if it’s just for a moment. Some days the hurt is sharp, other days it’s just a dull ache in the background. But as time passes, that pain starts to soften. New joys begin to appear, new dreams slowly take shape, and—little by little—life starts to feel possible again.
Over the months, she learned to honor her grief. To see it as a teacher instead of a curse. She found that loss could actually open her heart, deepen her compassion, and connect her to others in unexpected ways. Letting go became her path to freedom—a way to make peace with her past, and open herself to whatever comes next.
At some point, everyone faces loss. It’s never easy. But maybe, just maybe, grief is a tribute to love. A reminder that this life is precious—and that every ending carries the seed of a new beginning.

Chapter 9: Building a Life Rooted in Integrity and Self-Compassion
After all the storms and upheaval, there comes this quieter season—a time when you get to pause, rebuild, and really think about what comes next. It can feel like the hardest part, can’t it? The old rules are gone, but the new ones haven’t shown up yet. There’s this sense that anything’s possible, but also a lot of uncertainty. How do you create a life that feels genuine and true, when so much has been stripped away?
For one woman, her answer started with the smallest, everyday choices. She discovered that integrity wasn’t about being perfect—it was about living in alignment. Simply put, it meant making sure her actions matched her values, her beliefs, and what she wanted most deep down. It was about telling the truth, even when it felt awkward, and keeping promises to herself—not just to everyone else.
And self-compassion? That became her anchor. She learned to treat herself with the same kindness she’d easily give a friend. When she stumbled, she forgave herself. When she felt lost, she reminded herself that growth is often messy and unpredictable. She stopped measuring her worth by how much she got done, how she looked, or whether she was pleasing everybody.
Think about it—most of us are way harder on ourselves than we’d ever be on someone else. We carry around old stories of failure, shame, and regret. But here’s the real truth: everyone is doing the best they can with what they know. Self-compassion isn’t about letting yourself off the hook. It’s the rich soil where real change can actually grow.
Building a life grounded in integrity meant making choices that felt right, even when they were unpopular. It meant saying no to things that left her drained, and yes to the things that truly nourished her. She learned to trust that her own happiness mattered—not just for her own sake, but for everyone she connected with.
Over time, she found a new kind of peace. Not because all her struggles disappeared, but because she accepted herself, flaws and all. She realized she could be both strong and gentle, ambitious and content. This life she was building? It wasn’t perfect, but it was deeply, truly hers.
Deep down, most people long for this kind of wholeness. They want to feel at home in their own skin, to live honestly and kindly. The path isn’t always clear, but it starts with one simple, gentle step: choosing to treat yourself with the care and respect you truly deserve.

Chapter 10. Living Untamed: The Ongoing Practice of Freedom
You know, freedom isn’t really a place you arrive at—it's a way of living. It’s something you have to choose, over and over, especially when fear or doubt start to creep in. The world? Well, it’s always going to offer up new cages and fresh rules, tempting us to play small. But that invitation to live untamed? It’s always there, waiting.
For one woman, this journey was anything but finished. Every single day brought its own challenges—little nudges to fit in, to play it safe, to let comfort win out over courage. Some mornings, she woke up feeling strong and sure of herself. Other days, she stumbled. But she always came back to that one question that started it all: What if there’s more to life than this?
That’s really what living untamed is about. It’s about staying curious, keeping your heart open, and being true to who you are—even when your inner voice whispers things you’d rather not hear. It’s trusting that your dreams, your needs, and your boundaries actually matter.
Most people think freedom is some big, dramatic escape—a one-time event that changes everything. But honestly, it’s a bunch of small choices you make every day. It’s choosing to speak up, to rest when you need it, to play, to love, to let go, and to forgive—not just others, but yourself too. It’s about being willing to start fresh, no matter how many times you trip along the way.
Over time, her courage started to ripple out. The more authentic she became, the more others found the permission to question, to hope, and even to change. She realized something powerful—the best thing she could ever give the world was her own truth.
The journey of becoming untamed? It’s never really done. There’ll always be new fears, new challenges, and new chances to grow. But with every step you take, the world opens up a little more. It gets brighter. And most of all, it feels just a bit more free.

As we wrap up, just take a moment and let this sink in—walking the path of untaming isn’t a one-time leap. It’s a practice you carry with you, a way of living that invites you to question, to listen, to really feel, and to choose—again and again. Sure, it’s not always easy. But every step really is worth it. So, as you set out from here, hold on to a few gentle reminders: Your inner voice? It’s wise—so trust it, even if it feels unfamiliar at first. Sometimes, honoring your own truth means letting someone else down—and that’s okay. Remember, joy and pleasure aren’t just nice-to-haves; they’re essential for a full and vibrant life. If you’re grieving, let yourself feel it. Grief is proof of love, and healing follows when you give yourself that space. And, above all, self-compassion is what makes real, lasting change possible. Here’s something important—you're not walking this path alone. Every person who chooses to live untamed is lighting the way for someone else. There’ll be days when you feel lost or when those old rules start tugging you back. You might even hear that whisper of fear, telling you it’s safer to stay small. On those days, come back to your breath, to your body, to that quiet knowing deep inside. You don’t need to have it all figured out. You don’t have to be perfect, or fearless, or endlessly strong. All you really need is the willingness to listen, to try, and to start again when you need to. The world needs your wildness, your honesty, your hope. When you choose to live untamed, you’re giving everyone around you permission to do the same. So, take that next step—even if it’s a small one. Trust that your life is yours to shape. And know that freedom—in all its messy, beautiful forms—is always within reach.
